Śaunaka
------------------------------------------
Śaunaka is the name of a sage found in our ancient religious literature in many places (vide Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.5.3.5; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.20; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 4.7; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.3; Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3).
His original name was गृत्समद and came to be known as शौनक since he was the son of the sage Śunaka. He was considered a reincarnation of इन्द्र, the king of gods.
He was the author of several works most of which were centred round the Ṛgveda. They are known as Anukramaṇīs (indices). (See ANUKRAMAṆĪ.)
His magnum opus is the Bṛhaddevatā dealing with the Vedic deities. (See BṚHADDEVATĀ for details.)
Āśvalāyana was his chief disciple.
He was a कुलपति (supreme head of a gururkula or a residential forest university) with ten thousand Vedic students under his care.
According to the पुराणस् there was another Śaunaka—also known as Indrota—who made the king जनमेजय (son of Puru, of the lunar race) perform the अश्वमेध sacrifice to get rid of brahmahatyādoṣa (the sin of killing a ब्राह्मण).
See also ĀŚVALĀYANA.

Saundaryalaharī
(‘Wave of beauty’)
------------------------------------------
Apart from writing learned bhāṣyas or commentaries on recondite scriptures like the उपनिषद्स् and philosophical works like the Brahmasūtras, शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) also composed a number of beautiful stotras or hymns on the various deities of the Hindu pantheon. The Saundaryalaharī is one of his most famous hymns.
According to orthodox traditions, शङ्कर got the first 41 verses from कैलास, the abode of शिव and composed another 59, to make the total of 100.
As per another version, शङ्कर as a child was breastfed by the Divine मोथेर् (Tripurasundarī) herself, because of which he gained great spiritual power as well as the power to compose poetry (vide verse 74).
Though the first part comprising 41 verses is more commonly known as the Ānandalaharī and only the second part—the rest, 59 verses—as the Saundarya-laharī, the whole hymn is now generally called by the latter name.
The speciality of this composition is that it reflects equally the three important aspects of हिन्दुइस्म्, viz., Vedānta, devotion to the deity through the hymn, and the esoteric science of the mantras and yantras (mystic diagrams).
A brief account of the first part is as follows:
Verses Subject
1 and 2 The देवी is the creatrix.
3 to 8; 22; 27; 30 Various traditions of meditation on her.
31 to 33 Description of the श्रीचक्र.
9; 10; 14; 21 Meditation on the कुण्डलिनी.
12; 24 to 26; 28; 29 Greatness of श्रीविद्या.
13; 15 to 20 On cupidity.
23; 34 Meditation on the unified form of शिव and शक्ति.
35 Evolution of the world.
36 to 41 Meditation on the deity in the six चक्रस्.

The second part (verses 42 to 100) describes the physical form and beauty of the देवी in great detail.
Experts of the tradition of श्रीविद्या (science of worship and meditation on the Divine मोथेर्) have prescribed detailed procedures for worshipping the देवी through different yantras along with the repetition of the respective verses (a thousand times each), to secure various results. These have to be learnt from a qualified गुरु.
This hymn has 36 commentaries out of which Lakṣmīdharā of लक्ष्मीधर-deśika, Saubhāgyavardhinī of Kaivalyā-śrama and Aruṇāmodinī of कामेश्वर-sūrin are considered more important.

Śaunaka-smṛti
------------------------------------------
Śaunaka as an author of a स्मृति has been mentioned even by the Manusmṛti (3.16). His work has not been traced till now.
A work called Praṇavakalpa with a commentary of हेमाद्रि (13th century A. D.) is known to have existed.
Numerous works are attributed to शौनक. However, it is difficult to say whether they are by the same person. Some of these are: Arkavivāhapaddhati; Ekadaṇḍisaṁnyāsavidhi; Adbhutotpatti-śānti; Jīvacchrāddhaprayoga and Prayoga-pārijāta.
See also ŚAUNAKA.
